n:
- *a record of the ancestors*: This phrase introduces {{Matthew 1:1-17|1:1–17}}. A similar phrase appears in Genesis to start each section of that book. 

- *Jesus … David … Abraham*: These names repeat in reverse order in the list of Jesus' ancestors. This is a literary form called *chiasm* (arrangement of elements in mirror-image). Identifying Jesus as a descendant of David introduces him as the Messiah (see {{Matthew 12:23|Matthew 12:23}}; {{Matthew 22:42-45|22:42–45}}). The link to Abraham emphasizes God's promise to Israel and how the covenant (agreement) extends to include all nations (see {{Matthew 28:16-20|Matthew 28:16–20}}; {{Genesis 12:3|Genesis 12:3}}).

For Jews in Jesus’ time, family lines were very important.

Jesus’ family line shows that he was from Abraham’s family. He was also from the royal family of King David. Jews knew that the Messiah would come from these two family lines.

There are stories in the Old Testament about many of the people in Jesus’ family. Some of them are hard and painful stories. Some of these women and men weren’t from Israel. They were considered outsiders.

The family line recorded in the Gospel of Matthew showed something about Jesus. God’s promises in his covenant with Abraham are fulfilled through Jesus’ life and work. That is true about God’s promises in his covenant with David as well.

This family line showed that Jesus is the Messiah for all people. He is the Messiah for people who are Jews and people who aren’t Jews.

This story shows how certain parts of the life of Jesus fulfilled Old Testament prophecies. This includes: 

- his family history and birth (chapter {{Matthew 1:1-25|1}}), and 

- the places he lived as a child (chapter {{Matthew 2:1-23|2}}). 

The story also shows how efforts to stop the plan of God do not work ({{Matthew 2:1-15|2:1–15}}; see also {{Matthew 27:62-66|27:62–66}}).

Rahab was a Gentile prostitute who risked her life to hide the two spies of Joshua in Jericho ({{Joshua 2:1-21|Joshua 2:1–21}}). Her place in the Messiah's family tree emphasizes the grace of God. She is praised for her faith in Israel's God and her good actions ({{Hebrews 11:31|Hebrews 11:31}}; {{James 2:25|James 2:25}}).

*Asa* (Greek *Asaph*): this likely refers to the Old Testament king ({{1 Kings 15:9-24|1 Kings 15:9–24}}; {{1 Chronicles 3:10|1 Chronicles 3:10}}) and not the psalmist Asaph ({{1 Chronicles 6:39|1 Chronicles 6:39}}; {{1 Chronicles 25:1-2|25:1–2}}; {{Psalm 50:1-23|Psalms 50}}, {{Psalm 73:1-83:18|73–83}}). Matthew focuses on the family line from David to the Messiah.

*father of* (or *ancestor of*): Here this term refers to multiple generations ({{2 Chronicles 21:1-26|2 Chronicles 21:1–26:1}}). The same is true for Josiah ({{Matthew 1:11|Matthew 1:11}}) and Shealtiel ({{Matthew 1:12|1:12}}). The family line skips Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah ({{2 Kings 8:24|2 Kings 8:24}}; {{1 Chronicles 3:11|1 Chronicles 3:11}}; {{2 Chronicles 22:1|2 Chronicles 22:1}}, {{2 Chronicles 22:11|11}}; {{2 Chronicles 24:27|24:27}}). Perhaps this is because of their connection to Ahab and Jezebel.
The Old Testament is clearly the source for {{Matthew 1:1-11|Matthew 1:1–11}}. Matthew probably also used royal records and oral traditions for {{Matthew 1:12-16|1:12–16}}.
This family history follows Joseph, who is part of the family line of King David (see also study note on Luke 3:23–38).

Matthew says each time period has fourteen generations. But the first and third periods list only thirteen. A traditional Jewish and Old Testament method would count King David in both the first and second groups. It would include Jesus in the third group. 

This suggests Matthew is probably emphasizing the *gematria* (a system where letters represent numbers). The letters in the Hebrew word *dawid* (meaning "David") add up to fourteen. Matthew is emphasizing Jesus’ credentials as the Messiah ({{Matthew 1:1|1:1}}).

- *Jesus Christ* (literally *Jesus the Christ*): *Christ* is not a personal name. *Christ* is a title that means "Messiah" or "God's chosen one."

- *pledged in marriage*: In Judaism, engagement (or betrothal) was a permanent relationship ({{Malachi 2:14|Malachi 2:14}}). It could only end through legal action. So, by law, Mary was Joseph’s wife and he was her husband (see {{Matthew 1:20|Matthew 1:20}}; {{Deuteronomy 22:23-24|Deuteronomy 22:23–24}}). This was true even though they had not had sexual relations. Since Mary was a virgin when the Holy Spirit conceived Jesus, it proves Jesus’ divine nature.

In the story of Jesus’ birth, Matthew recorded many things about who Jesus is. Jesus is the Messiah and he comes from God.

The Holy Spirit made it possible for Mary to be pregnant.

A spiritual being called an angel told Joseph about the baby.

This baby would be the Saviour of God’s people.

Words from the prophet Isaiah came true in Jesus’ life (Matthew 1:23).

Isaiah’s prophecy about Jesus showed that God is with his people through Jesus.

Jesus would bring the freedom and healing that God wanted to give them.

Joseph was a righteous man. This means he obeyed the law (see {{Luke 1:6|Luke 1:6}}). He reconsidered marrying Mary because it appeared she had committed adultery. He could have cleared his name by publicly accusing Mary. This would have led to her trial and possible execution ({{Deuteronomy 22:23-27|Deuteronomy 22:23–27}}; compare {{Numbers 5:11-31|Numbers 5:11–31}}). Or he could pay a fine and end the engagement (see also *Mishnah Sotah* 1:1–5). Joseph chose to be kind and decided to end the engagement quietly.

The angel of the Lord told Joseph in a dream (see {{Matthew 2:12-13|Matthew 2:12–13}}, {{Matthew 2:19|19}}, {{Matthew 2:22|22}}) that no one had seduced or harmed Mary. Instead, the baby was conceived by the Holy Spirit ({{Luke 1:34-35|Luke 1:34–35}}). The Holy Spirit often plays a creative and life-giving role ({{Genesis 1:2|Genesis 1:2}}; {{Ezekiel 37:1-14|Ezekiel 37:1–14}}; {{John 3:5-8|John 3:5–8}}).

- Jesus is the Greek version of the Hebrew name *Yeshua,* which means "The Lord saves." This name describes his role, that *he will save his people from their sins*. 

- *His people* may refer to either Israel as a nation ({{Matthew 2:6|Matthew 2:6}}) or to the Messiah’s people, the church. This includes both Jews and non-Jewish (Gentile) people ({{Matthew 4:15-16|4:15–16}}; {{Matthew 16:18|16:18}}; {{Matthew 28:18-20|28:18–20}}).

Jesus being born from a virgin fulfills {{Isaiah 7:14|Isaiah 7:14}}. The Hebrew word *‘almah* can mean “virgin” or “young woman.” In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it was translated as *parthenos* (“virgin”), which Matthew quotes. Matthew sees the *‘almah* in Isaiah as pointing forward to the Virgin Mary.

- *he had no union with her until she gave birth to a Son*: this might indicate that Joseph had sexual relations with Mary after Jesus was born. (Some traditions teach that Mary remained a virgin throughout her life.)

- Joseph named him Jesus, showing he accepted the child as his own.

- Bethlehem was King David’s hometown ({{1 Samuel 16:1-13|1 Samuel 16:1–13}}; {{John 7:42|John 7:42}}). 

- King Herod was also called "Herod the Great." He had a rapid increase in power. He went from being the governor of Galilee to the king of Galilee, Judea, and Samaria. He was king from 37–4 BC. He was very loyal to Rome. He was famous for impressive building projects. This included a major renovation of the Temple in Jerusalem. His rule also included family conflicts, suspicion, and the murder of his own family members and innocent children (Josephus, *Antiquities* 15.7.1–5; {{Matthew 2:16-18|Matthew 2:16–18}}).

The wise men's focus on the star shows they were astrologers. Their knowledge of the Old Testament (possibly {{Numbers 24:17|Numbers 24:17}}) suggests they came from Babylonia, where many Jews lived. These men were Gentiles (non-Jewish people), which hints at God accepting Gentiles in his kingdom ({{Matthew 8:11-12|Matthew 8:11–12}}; {{Matthew 15:21-28|15:21–28}}; {{Matthew 28:16-20|28:16–20}}). 

All through the Gospel, unlikely Gentiles worship the Jewish Messiah, while many Jewish leaders (Herod, the high priests, the teachers of religious law, and the Pharisees) oppose him.

Jesus was born into a poor family. He was born in a small town called Bethlehem. His birth wasn’t important news that everyone knew about.

But Matthew wrote about some signs that showed how important Jesus’ birth was. Wise Men announced that Jesus was a king. This made Herod the Great upset.

The emperor Caesar had made Herod the king of Judea. A new king would challenge his power. Herod was a mean and unkind ruler who did terrible things. He had many babies killed when he tried to kill Jesus.

But God protected the baby Jesus from Herod. Jesus’ parents escaped to Egypt. Later they lived in safety in Galilee.

Matthew often describes Jesus as receiving worshipped ({{Matthew 2:2|Matthew 2:2}}, {{Matthew 2:8|8}}, {{Matthew 2:11|11}}; {{Matthew 8:2|8:2}}; {{Matthew 9:18|9:18}}; {{Matthew 14:33|14:33}}; {{Matthew 15:25|15:25}}; {{Matthew 20:20|20:20}}; {{Matthew 28:9|28:9}}, {{Matthew 28:17|17}}). In this way, Matthew identifies Jesus as God.
It worried Herod very much because he thought this child might challenge him as King of the Jews.

The leading priests had political and religious influence and mainly served in the temple (see {{Matthew 21:23|Matthew 21:23}}). Herod gathered the teachers of religious law because they knew Old Testament prophecies and were often influential Pharisees.

- Bethlehem was a small village. It was important because it was where King David was born. The religious leaders knew from prophecy ({{Matthew 1:22|Matthew 1:22}}) that this is where God would cause his Messiah to be born there. 

- King David had been a shepherd when he was young. As king, he became the shepherd of Israel ({{2 Samuel 5:2|2 Samuel 5:2}}). {{Micah 5:2-4|Micah 5:2–4}} predicts the Messiah as a shepherd (compare {{Psalm 23:1|Psalm 23:1}}).
God placed the star to guide the wise men to the Messiah (see {{Numbers 24:17|Numbers 24:17}}). The details are unclear.

The wise men gave costly gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh to the king (see {{Psalm 72:10-17|Psalm 72:10–17}}; {{Isaiah 60:1-22|Isaiah 60}}). The idea of three wise men comes from the number of gifts. But the text does not say how many wise men there were.

*flee to Egypt … until I tell you*: This action fulfills the prophecy in {{Hosea 11:1|Hosea 11:1}} (refer to study note on Matthew 4:1–11; see also {{Genesis 15:13-16|Genesis 15:13–16}}; {{Genesis 46:1-5|46:1–5}}; {{Exodus 15:1-21|Exodus 15:1–21}}).
*Out of Egypt I called My Son*: See {{Hosea 11:1|Hosea 11:1}}, which refers to when God led the Israelites out of Egypt.

- *Put to death all the boys*: Herod was famous for his cruelty. He even killed his own son to protect his throne. This led to the saying, “It is safer to be Herod’s pig [Greek *hus*] than his son [Greek *huios*].” This is because Herod followed Jewish kosher laws. 

- *two years old and under*: Herod estimated the child's age based on the wise men’s report.
*Ramah* was a village near Bethlehem. It is where the patriarch Jacob buried his wife Rachel ({{Genesis 35:18-20|Genesis 35:18–20}}; {{Jeremiah 31:15-17|Jeremiah 31:15–17}}).

*After Herod died*: Herod the Great died in 4 BC. Caesar (the Roman emperor) divided his kingdom. Herod's son Archelaus ({{Matthew 2:22|Matthew 2:22}}) became ruler of Judea, Samaria, and Idumea. Herod Antipas ({{Matthew 14:1-12|14:1–12}}; {{Luke 13:31-32|Luke 13:31–32}}) took charge of Galilee and Perea.
Jesus returned to Israel to fulfill the prophecy in {{Hosea 11:1|Hosea 11:1}} (see {{Matthew 2:13-15|Hosea 2:13–15}}).

- Archelaus, like his father, ruled with cruelty, injustice, and harshness. 

- Joseph moved to Galilee to escape the control of Archelaus. This fulfilled a prophecy (see {{Matthew 4:12-16|Matthew 4:12–16}}).

“*He will be called a Nazarene*”: Matthew connects the name *Nazareth* with words from the prophets (see {{Isaiah 11:1|Isaiah 11:1}}, where the Messiah is called a “Branch,” [Hebrew netser]; and {{Judges 13:5|Judges 13:5}}, where Samson is called a “Nazirite”).

- John the Baptist announced the arrival of Jesus (see {{Mark 1:1-11|Mark 1:1–11}}; {{Luke 3:1-22|Luke 3:1–22}}; {{John 1:6-8|John 1:6–8}}, {{John 1:19-34|19–34}}). John helped people get ready to welcome him ({{Matthew 3:3|Matt 3:3}}). John drew large crowds ({{Matthew 3:5|3:5}}) and gathered a group of followers ({{Matthew 9:14|9:14}}). This group continued for a short time as a movement, even after the Christian church began (see {{Acts 18:24-28|Acts 18:24–28}}). 

- John lived in the Judean wilderness. This was symbolic because the wilderness linked to God giving the law (see {{Exodus 19:1|Exodus 19:1}}). It also related to God's final redemption of Israel at the end of time (see {{Isaiah 40:3|Isaiah 40:3}}).

John the Baptist was the messenger who came before the Messiah. In many ways he was like the prophets from long ago.

He wore clothing like the prophet Elijah had worn (2 Kings 1:8). His message was also like Elijah’s message. He told people how to prepare for the Lord to come.

Also like Elijah, John went out into the desert and then to the River Jordan. One person after another turned away from sin and was baptised because of John’s preaching.

Yet John the Baptist’s work wasn’t only about individual people. He was preparing the community for God’s arrival. He expected the Messiah to come and to bring judgement and salvation.

The prophetic call to return to God means turning away from pride and sin and choosing humble obedience to God (compare {{Isaiah 1:16-20|Isaiah 1:16–20}} and {{Jeremiah 3:11-22|Jeremiah 3:11–22}}). John’s message included specific practical advice ({{Luke 3:11-14|Luke 3:11–14}}).

Isaiah talked about someone making a path in the desert for God to come back to Israel ({{Isaiah 40:1-11|Isaiah 40:1–11}}). John's work got things ready for Jesus to arrive (see {{Matthew 11:10|Matthew 11:10}}; compare {{John 12:41|John 12:41}}).
John wore the same kind of clothes and ate the same kind of food as Elijah, a prophet who had lived many years before ({{2 Kings 1:8|2 Kings 1:8}}; {{Malachi 4:5|Malachi 4:5}}; *Sirach *48:10–11).

- John's ministry became so popular that many people from Jerusalem and Judea came to hear him. 

- *Confessing their sins*: Those who listened to John's preaching and turned away from sin were ready to accept the ministry of Jesus ({{Luke 7:27|Luke 7:27}}, {{Luke 7:29|29}}). 

- *they were baptized*: John's practice of baptism might have started with the Old Testament idea of purification (see {{Isaiah 1:16|Isaiah 1:16}}; {{Isaiah 4:4|4:4}}; {{Ezekiel 36:25|Ezekiel 36:25}}).

- The Pahrisees' name comes from the Hebrew word *perushim*, which means *separated ones* or *exact interpreters*. 

- The Sadducees, a group of priests, probably got their name from Zadok the priest ({{2 Samuel 15:24-29|2 Samuel 15:24–29}}; {{Ezekiel 44:10-16|Ezekiel 44:10–16}}).

*Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance*: John calls for action and real ethical change. Only talking about it is not enough (see {{Luke 3:10-14|Luke 3:10–14}}; compare {{Matthew 5:19-20|Matthew 5:19–20}}, {{Matthew 5:46|46}}; {{Matthew 7:21|7:21}}; {{Matthew 23:3|23:3}}).

- *Do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father’*: Some people had wrong assumptions. They thought that being descendants of Abraham meant they were free from God's judgment. 

- A key theme in Matthew is that God will create new children of Abraham. He will include non-Jews (Gentiles) in God's people. He will remove Jews who reject the Messiah (see {{Matthew 8:11-12|8:11–12}}; {{Matthew 21:43|21:43}}; {{Matthew 22:1-14|22:1–14}}; {{Matthew 28:16-20|28:16–20}}; {{Romans 4:9-25|Romans 4:9–25}}; {{Galatians 3:6-14|Galatians 3:6–14}}, {{Galatians 3:29|29}}).

- *One more powerful than I*: Even though he was popular and many people continued to follow him, John knew he was less important than the Messiah. 

- *whose sandals I am not worthy to carry*: In Jewish culture, removing and carrying sandals was a task for slaves. Not even a rabbi's disciple would do it. 

- *with the Holy Spirit and with fire*: This happened at Pentecost (see {{Joel 2:28-29|Joel 2:28–29}}; {{Acts 2:1-47|Acts 2:1–47}}). This may include the ministry of Jesus, empowered by the Holy Spirit (see {{Matthew 12:28|Matthew 12:28}}; {{Luke 4:14|Luke 4:14}}). Fire could mean purification ({{Zechariah 13:9|Zech 13:9}}) or judgment ({{Malachi 3:2-3|Malachi 3:2–3;}}{{Malachi 4:1|4:1}}; see {{Isaiah 1:25|Isaiah 1:25}}; {{Isaiah 4:4|4:4}}). It is a “Spirit-and-fire baptism.” The Messiah completes what John could only start (full judgment and purification).

Farmers used a winnowing fork to throw harvested grain into the air, letting the useless husks (chaff) blow away. 

The Messiah's work separates humanity into two groups: 

- the *wheat*, those who respond and become God's new people; and

- the *chaff*, those who refuse to repent (see {{Matthew 3:8|Matthew 3:8}}).

Jesus hadn’t sinned, so John the Baptist didn’t expect to baptise him.

Jesus was baptised to show that he was one of the people of Israel. It also showed that he agreed with John the Baptist’s message.

At Jesus’ baptism, God made himself known as the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. These are the three persons of the Trinity.

The Spirit of God came down as a dove. This was a sign of the peace that the Messiah was offering.

Then the Father announced the truth about Jesus. Jesus is the Son of God and God loves him.

These signs helped Jesus prepare to do his work for God and others.
John had already admitted ({{Matthew 3:11-12|Matthew 3:11–12}}) that he was less important than the Messiah, so he felt unworthy to baptize him.

*“It is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness in this way”*: This means completing what the Old Testament required or prophesied (for example, {{Jeremiah 31:31-34|Jeremiah 31:31–34}}). In Matthew, “righteousness” means acting according to God’s will (see {{Matthew 5:20|Matthew 5:20}}; {{Matthew 6:1|6:1}}, {{Matthew 6:33|33}}; {{Matthew 21:32|21:32}}).

The Spirit of God came down like a dove to anoint Jesus, who would bring salvation. This was similar to a king being anointed with oil at his crowning. The Holy Spirit gave Jesus the strength to achieve God's salvation and defeat Satan (see {{Matthew 12:18|Matthew 12:18}}, {{Matthew 12:28|28}}). This same Spirit gives strength to the disciples of Jesus ({{Matthew 10:20|10:20}}; {{Acts 1:8|Acts 1:8}}).

- *This is My beloved Son* (see {{Psalm 2:7|Psalm 2:7}}): The title “Son of God” explains the nature and role of Jesus (see {{Matthew 4:3|Matthew 4:3}}, {{Matthew 4:6|6}}; {{Matthew 14:33|14:33}}; {{Matthew 16:16|16:16}}; {{Matthew 17:5|17:5}}; {{Matthew 26:63|26:63}}; {{Matthew 27:54|27:54}}; {{Matthew 28:19|28:19}}). In his special relationship with God the Father, Jesus achieves salvation as the faithful and obedient Son. 

- *in whom I am well pleased*: God the Father confirmed his Son’s work with words from Isaiah ({{Isaiah 42:1|Isaiah 42:1}}) and prepared Israel for the work of Jesus.

- *Jesus was led by the Spirit*: God arranged this test to examine the Messiah’s character (see {{Deuteronomy 8:2|Deuteronomy 8:2}}). 

- *to be tempted by the devil*: God started this test of character, using the devil's wish to lead Jesus into sin. God tempts no one ({{James 1:13-14|James 1:13–14}}).

Jesus went to the desert. This helped him prepare to start doing his work among people. Right away the devil came to tempt him.

The devil wanted to keep his power to do evil things in the world. But his power was in danger because Jesus had come to earth. Jesus had come to stop the power of sin, death and evil.

The devil tempted Jesus to find help and strength in something other than God. He wanted Jesus to turn stones into bread. If Jesus did that, he would be providing for his own needs. He wouldn’t be trusting God to provide for him.

The devil tempted Jesus to jump down from the temple. The devil said that this would show everyone how powerful Jesus was. If Jesus did that, he would be acting with pride. He would be seeking glory for himself. He wouldn’t be trusting God to honour him.

Then the devil offered to give Jesus all the riches of the world. But if Jesus worshipped the devil, he couldn’t serve and worship only God. Each time the devil tempted him, Jesus answered using words from the book of Deuteronomy.

In Deuteronomy Moses had urged God’s people to be faithful to the Mount Sinai covenant. The Israelites didn’t listen to Moses or stay faithful to God’s covenant. Unlike them, Jesus did remain faithful to God. The devil left Jesus. But he kept trying to stop Jesus’ work.

This story of the temptation of Jesus shows clear parallels between Adam and Jesus. Jesus is the second Adam (see {{Romans 5:12-19|Romans 5:12–19}}) and the second Israel ({{Matthew 2:15|Matthew 2:15}}). Unlike the ancient Israelites, Jesus completed Israel’s history by wandering through the desert without sinning. He showed he was the obedient Son of God by defeating Satan in spiritual battle. 

Since Jesus faced temptation as a human, he can understand the temptations we encounter (see {{Hebrews 2:14-18|Hebrews 2:14–18}}; {{Hebrews 4:15|4:15}}). He helps us overcome them as he did ({{1 Corinthians 10:13|1 Corinthians 10:13}}).

*Forty days and forty nights* (see {{Exodus 24:18|Exodus 24:18}}; {{Exodus 34:28|34:28}}; {{1 Kings 19:8|1 Kings 19:8}}): God tested Israel for forty-years in the wilderness ({{Exodus 16:35|Exodus 16:35}}; {{Deuteronomy 1:3|Deuteronomy 1:3}}).

Jesus refused to use his supernatural power to get food, trusting God to provide it. The people of Israel relentlessly tested God with complaints and disbelief (see {{Exodus 16:1-36|Exodus 16}}). But, Jesus refused to doubt God's faithfulness. Instead, he relied on God to meet his real need. This was the spiritual provision that comes from every word of God.
Jesus refused to test God by assuming God would always protect him.
*It is also written*: Jesus responded to the devil's use of Scripture by emphasizing a more important principle (honoring God) which the devil ignored.

- Satan is called "the prince of this world" in {{John 12:31|John 12:31}}. He offered Jesus control over all the world's kingdoms and their power. Satan did this to try to stop Jesus from fulfilling God's will. 

- *Glory* means political power and control (for example, {{Matthew 6:29|Matthew 6:29}}). Satan planned to tempt Jesus to misuse his divine nature as Son. He wanted to distract him from the path of suffering and obedience that led to the crucifixion.

- *Then the devil left Him*: Jesus rejected Satan. This points ahead to his later victories over demons ({{Matthew 12:28|Matthew 12:28}}), Satan's defeat through the cross ({{Colossians 2:14-15|Colossians 2:14–15}}), and the final victory at the end of time ({{Romans 16:20|Romans 16:20}}; {{Revelation 12:7-17|Revelation 12:7–17}}; {{Revelation 20:2-3|20:2–3}}, {{Revelation 20:10|10}}). 

- Angels had already been part of the Messiah's arrival and protection ({{Matthew 1:20|Matthew 1:20}}, {{Matthew 1:24|24}}; {{Matthew 2:13|2:13}}, {{Matthew 2:19|19}}). Now they came and cared for Jesus after his temptation, fulfilling the Old Testament ({{Matthew 4:6|4:6}}; see {{Psalm 91:11-12|Psalm 91:11–12}}).

- Herod Antipas was the ruler of Galilee and Perea. He had arrested John the Baptist (see {{Matthew 14:1-12|14:1–12}}). John was probably working in the area at this time. 

- When Jesus heard about this, he left Judea. This was near Perea, where Herod had John arrested. Jesus then went back to Galilee. Jesus left to avoid death before he could finish his mission of revealing God's Kingdom. Like Joseph's escape to Nazareth ({{Matthew 2:22-23|Matthew 2:22–23}}), avoiding danger can also be part of God's plan and fulfill prophecy ({{Matthew 4:14-16|4:14–16}}).

God had promised that he would send his people a new ruler. Prophets from hundreds of years before had announced this message. The new ruler would come through David’s family line (Isaiah 9:7).

Matthew showed that Jesus was that ruler. Jesus was from Galilee. Galilee was the place Isaiah had prophesied about. And Jesus brought God’s light.

The prophet Isaiah talked about people living in darkness. This was a way of describing what sin does to people. It controls them so they can’t see who God is or enjoy his goodness.

But Matthew showed that there was a great light was shining on people. Jesus was the light that showed people what God is like. He showed them what it meant to live for God. They started by turning away from sin.

Through Jesus, God was bringing his rule to earth. That is what Jesus meant about the kingdom of heaven being near. The kingdom of heaven is the kingdom of God.

John the Baptist and the Father announced Jesus as the Messiah ({{Matthew 3:13-17|3:13–17}}). He then endured testing in the wilderness with obedience ({{Matthew 4:1-11|4:1–11}}). After this, the Messiah was ready to begin his work. He first preached the message of the kingdom of God to the people of Galilee.

Capernaum was in Galilee, a region that the religious leaders in Judea and Jerusalem viewed negatively (see {{John 1:46|John 1:46}}; {{John 7:41-42|7:41–42}}, {{John 7:52|52}}). Many people from Judea thought Galileans to be unrefined and poorly spoken (compare {{Matthew 26:73|Matt 26:73}}). The leaders believed these people could make their teachings less accurate. Galilee also had more non-Jewish people than Judea.
Jesus taught that the kingdom of heaven was coming soon and urged people to repent (stop doing what is wrong) in preparation (see {{Matthew 3:2|Matthew 3:2}}; {{Matthew 10:7|10:7}}).

Simon, also known as Peter, became the leader of the apostles (see {{Matthew 14:28|14:28}}; {{Matthew 15:15|15:15}}; {{Matthew 16:16|16:16}}) and the representative disciple ({{Matthew 14:29-30|14:29–30}}; {{Matthew 16:15-19|16:15–19}}, {{Matthew 16:22-23|22–23}}).

The call of the first disciples shows one purpose of the ministry of Jesus: to invite people to follow him with self-denying obedience (compare {{Matthew 4:17|Matthew 4:17}}, {{Matthew 4:23-25|23–25}}).

Jesus had work to do for the kingdom of God. He began this work by asking certain people to be his disciples. The disciples would join Jesus in his work and learn from him.

Peter, Andrew, James and John saw that Jesus had authority. They left their work as fishermen and followed Jesus at once.

Jesus’ work included teaching and healing. He taught that God is the true King of the world. Through Jesus, God had come to save people. He came to save them from the power of sin, death and evil. This was good news!

Jesus acted with power to make many people strong and healthy. The miracles he did showed that God is stronger than illness and pain. They showed that God is stronger than evil spiritual beings like demons. People heard about these mighty works and were excited. Large crowds gathered around Jesus.

- *Come, follow Me*: This meant accepting the beliefs and lifestyle of a teacher as your own ({{Matthew 16:24|Matthew 16:24}}; {{Deuteronomy 5:33|Deuteronomy 5:33}}; {{1 Kings 19:19-21|1 Kings 19:19–21}}). 

- *fishers of men*: The disciples would help in the saving and judging work of the kingdom of heaven (see {{Matthew 10:5-15|Matthew 10:5–15}}; {{Matthew 13:47-51|13:47–51}}; {{Ezekiel 29:4-5|Ezekiel 29:4–5}}; {{Amos 4:2|Amos 4:2}}).

*They left the boat and their father*: To be disciples of Jesus required both commitment and sacrifice from the brothers (see {{Matthew 8:18-22|Matthew 8:18–22}}; {{Matthew 10:38|10:38}}; {{Matthew 16:24|16:24}}; {{Matthew 19:21|19:21}}).

- The Messiah's work focuses on three main activities: *teaching … preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing*.

- The *synagogues* were Jewish places for prayer, study, and discussing Scripture and tradition. They were also the social centers of many Jewish villages. The hypocrisy and hostility of Jewish leaders were obvious in the synagogues ({{Matthew 6:2|Matthew 6:2}}, {{Matthew 6:5|5}}; {{Matthew 10:17|10:17}}; {{Matthew 12:9-14|12:9–14}}; {{Matthew 13:54|13:54}}; {{Matthew 23:6|23:6}}, {{Matthew 23:34|34}}).

- *Preaching the gospel* involves sharing the message about the kingdom of heaven ({{Matthew 9:35|9:35}}; {{Matthew 24:14|24:14}}; {{Matthew 26:13|26:13}}; also {{Mark 1:1|Mark 1:1}}; {{Romans 1:16|Romans 1:16}}). This message often causes hostility (see {{Matthew 9:32-34|Matthew 9:32–34}}; {{Matthew 10:27-28|10:27–28}}; {{Matthew 13:1-9|13:1–9}}, {{Matthew 13:18-23|18–23}}).

This summary highlights the main theme of the section ({{Matthew 4:23-9:38|Matthew 4:23–9:38}}): the work and message of the Messiah. In ancient writings, chapters did not exist. Authors would start and end a section with the same phrase (called an *inclusio*; see {{Matthew 9:35|9:35}}).

- During the time of Jesus, much of Palestine was under Roman control as part of Syria. At that time, Syria could mean the whole eastern Mediterranean coast. Matthew mentions Syria to show how far news of Jesus spread.

- *those having seizures*: This refers to epilepsy or demonic possession. In {{Matthew 17:15|17:15}}, a person described this way "falls into the fire for into the water," meaning the boy could not control himself.

- *The Decapolis* was a group of ten cities, mostly east of the Jordan River and southeast of the Sea of Galilee. These included: 

- Damascus, 

- Raphana, 

- Hippos, 

- Abila (or Canatha), 

- Gadara, 

- Scythopolis, 

- Pella, 

- Dion, 

- Gerasa, and 

- Philadelphia (Amman). 

These cities were mostly Gentile (non-Jewish) and followed Greek culture.

This was the first of Jesus’ long messages. The message began with Jesus gathering his disciples together on a mountainside. He taught them how to live as part of the kingdom of heaven.

He started by saying what kind of people would be part of the kingdom of heaven. This kingdom is very different from how human kingdoms or governments work. It isn’t for people who are proud and think they don’t need God. It isn’t for people who use their strength to make others suffer. It isn’t for people who are only committed to their own happiness.

Jesus knows that many people have been treated badly and are suffering. Many are sad. Many know that they need God’s help. Many people are longing for justice and peace to fill the earth. Many understand what God cares deeply about. They do what God wants done even when it’s hard.

Jesus said all these people are blessed. They are God’s children. He will comfort them and show them mercy. They are part of the kingdom of heaven.

This is the first of five long teachings in Matthew (see also {{Matthew 9:35-11:1|9:35–11:1}}; {{Matthew 13:1-53|13:1–53}}; {{Matthew 18:1-19:2|18:1–19:2}}; {{Matthew 23:1-26|23:1–26:1}}). The Sermon on the Mount focuses on the Messiah's call for people to become righteousness. Paul considered righteousness to be God's saving actions and a person's status before God. Jesus uses the term to mean moral behavior that obeys God's will, like the apostle James. *Righteousness* means doing God's will as Jesus reveals it. This "revelation of righteousness" connects the whole sermon.

*The poor in spirit* (compare {{Luke 6:20|Luke 6:20}}, {{Luke 6:24|24}}): in the Old Testament, the poor are often shown as very devoted to God because the rich oppress them. This oppression leads them to trust in the Lord for salvation and help, instead of relying on wealth ({{Matthew 11:5|Matthew 11:5}}; {{Psalm 37:14-15|Psalms 37:14–15}}; {{Psalm 40:17|40:17}}; {{Psalm 69:28-33|69:28–33}}; {{Isaiah 61:1|Isaiah 61:1}}; {{Isaiah 66:2|66:2}}). 

In both Matthew’s and Luke’s writings, the “poor” are indeed financially poor, but their trust in God, not their poverty, makes them blessed ({{Isaiah 57:15|Isaiah 57:15}}; {{Isaiah 66:2|66:2}}).

- *Those who mourn* are the people who felt sad about Israel's spiritual and national condition (see {{Matthew 23:37-39|Matthew 23:37–39}}; {{Isaiah 61:2-3|Isaiah 61:2–3}}; {{Joel 1:8-13|Joel 1:8–13}}; {{Joel 2:12-13|2:12–13}}, {{Joel 2:18-19|18–19}}; {{Romans 9:1-5|Romans 9:1–5}}; {{1 Corinthians 5:2|1 Corinthians 5:2}}; {{James 4:9|James 4:9}}). It may also include to personal sorrow, whether from sin or tragedy ({{Mark 16:10|Mark 16:10}}; {{Revelation 18:11|Revelation 18:11}}, {{Revelation 18:19|19}}).

- *will be comforted*: The passive voice shows respect for God's holy name. It could also mean God *will comfort them* (see also {{Matthew 5:6-7|Matthew 5:6–7}}, {{Matthew 5:9|9}}). Comfort will come when God fulfills all his promises ({{Isaiah 40:1-2|Isaiah 40:1–2}}; {{Isaiah 61:2-3|61:2–3}}).

- *the meek: *Jesus almost directly quotes {{Psalm 37:11|Psalm 37:11}}here. In other places, Jesus describes himself in a similar way, contrasting with other teachers ({{Matthew 11:29|Matthew 11:29}}). He also avoids pride ({{Matthew 12:17-21|Matthew 12:17–21}}; {{Matthew 21:5|Matthew 21:5}}). Jesus shows this trait through his death on the cross ({{1 Peter 2:23|1 Peter 2:23}}; {{1 Peter 3:9|1 Peter 3:9}}).

- The whole earth could also mean *the land*, referring to God's promise of land to Abraham and his descendants ({{Genesis 12:7|Genesis 12:7}}; {{Genesis 17:8|Genesis 17:8}}; see {{Isaiah 60:21|Isaiah 60:21}}). It might also mean God's rule over the entire earth ({{Matthew 19:28|Matthew 19:28}}; {{Matthew 28:18-20|Matthew 28:18–20}}; {{Psalm 115:16|Psalm 115:16}}).

- *Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness*: These are either followers of Jesus whose main purpose in life is to obey him (see {{Matthew 3:15|Matthew 3:15}}; {{Matthew 5:10|5:10}}, {{Matthew 5:20|20}}), or they could be people who want justice for everyone ({{Psalm 11:7|Psalms 11:7}}; {{Psalm 85:10-12|85:10–12}}; {{Isaiah 11:1-4|Isaiah 11:1–4}}; {{Jeremiah 23:5-6|Jeremiah 23:5–6}}; {{Jeremiah 33:16|33:16}}). They often pray, “Your will be done, on earth” ({{Matthew 6:10|Matthew 6:10}}).

- Christ has brought justice and righteousness ({{Romans 3:21-22|Romans 3:21–22}}; {{Romans 5:1|5:1}}), and his followers will find satisfaction in it (compare {{Psalm 42:1-2|Psalms 42:1–2}}; {{Psalm 63:1-2|63:1–2}}).

Jesus emphasized the great importance of being merciful. This means to show kindness to those in need (see {{Matthew 6:12|Matthew 6:12}}, {{Matthew 6:14-15|14–15}}; {{Matthew 9:13|9:13}}; {{Matthew 12:7|12:7}}; {{Matthew 18:23-35|18:23–35}}; {{Matthew 23:23|23:23}}; {{Matthew 25:31-46|25:31–46}}). Those who are merciful now will receive God's mercy at the final judgment.

- *The pure in heart* (see {{Psalm 24:3-5|Psalms 24:3–5}}; {{Psalm 51:7|51:7}}; {{Isaiah 6:5|Isaiah 6:5}}) differ from those who believed they could please God by following human traditions (see {{Matthew 23:25-26|Matthew 23:25–26}}). Jesus emphasized simple, genuine righteousness from within (see {{Matthew 6:1-24|6:1–24}}; {{Matthew 15:1-20|15:1–20}}; {{Matthew 23:23-28|23:23–28}}; {{Deuteronomy 6:5|Deuteronomy 6:5}}).

- *They will see God* and achieve more than Moses did (see {{Exodus 33:18-23|Exodus 33:18–23}}; {{Exodus 34:5-7|34:5–7}}; see also {{Psalm 73:1|Psalm 73:1}}).

- This teaching likely addressed zealots. These were Jewish revolutionaries who wanted to overthrow Roman rule with violence. The Messiah’s kingdom would come through different methods.

- *the peacemakers*: Jesus was not calling for complete pacifism. Instead, he called for a new kind of action.

- Peace means no hostility and the presence of God’s salvation ({{Leviticus 26:6|Leviticus 26:6}}; {{1 Samuel 16:4-5|1 Samuel 16:4–5}}; {{Isaiah 9:5-6|Isaiah 9:5–6}}; {{Zechariah 8:16|Zechariah 8:16}}; {{Ephesians 2:14|Ephesians 2:14}}; {{Colossians 1:20|Colossians 1:20}}). Those who follow Jesus should work for justice, righteousness, reconciliation, and mercy. These should be the *effects* of God’s salvation through Christ ({{Matthew 5:43-47|Matthew 5:43–47}}; {{Luke 10:5-6|Luke 10:5–6}}).

The first followers of Jesus were persecuted by Jewish leaders who were offended by the new teaching of Jesus, which revealed God’s truth with authority (see {{Matthew 10:17-23|Matthew 10:17–23}}; {{Matthew 11:2-6|11:2–6}}; {{Matthew 12:1-8|12:1–8}}; {{Matthew 15:1-20|15:1–20}}; {{Matthew 23:34-36|23:34–36}}). Since then, following Jesus and his teachings has often led to persecution ({{Matthew 10:24-25|10:24–25}}; {{2 Timothy 3:12|2 Timothy 3:12}}).

- The *great … reward* Jesus talks about is not earned by suffering for doing right. It is God's blessing for those who show his grace to others (see {{Matthew 10:41-42|Matthew 10:41–42}}; {{Matthew 20:1-16|20:1–16}}). 

- The ancient *prophets* are closely connected with the New Testament apostles (see also {{Matthew 13:16-17|13:16–17}}; {{Matthew 23:29-36|23:29–36}}; {{Ephesians 2:20|Ephesians 2:20}}).

- People used salt for a number of reasons:

- to clean and prevent decay ({{Ezekiel 16:4|Ezekiel 16:4}}), 

- in making agreements ({{Leviticus 2:13|Leviticus 2:13}}; {{Numbers 18:19|Numbers 18:19}}; see study note on 2 Chronicles 13:5), and

- to flavor food ({{Job 6:6|Job 6:6}}; {{Mark 9:50|Mark 9:50}}).

- *Salt *that* loses its savor *becomes useless or tasteless (see {{Mark 9:50|Mark 9:50}}; {{Luke 14:34|Luke 14:34}}).
The good actions of the disciples will positively impact the world, bringing glory to God. Jesus warns them not to do anything that could harm this positive influence.

Jesus said that God’s people are to be salt and light in the world. He was talking about the way that they live. Salt keeps food from rotting and light makes darkness go away. God doesn’t want his world to rot away. He doesn’t want it to be in darkness because of sin. His people must live in ways that keep his world healthy and safe. That’s how they help other people groups and nations come to know and serve God.

Jesus loved God’s word. He taught people to respect and follow God’s instructions. This included the Law of Moses and the Prophets. Old Testament books of history, laws and prophecy talked about God ruling fully as King. That started to happen through Jesus. That is how the Old Testament Scriptures were fulfilled through Jesus.

*Light of the world … city on a hill*: How the disciples live will inspire others to live the same way and honor God (see {{Isaiah 2:2-5|Isaiah 2:2–5}}; {{Isaiah 42:6|42:6}}; {{Isaiah 49:6|49:6}}; {{Isaiah 51:4|51:4}}; {{Isaiah 56:6-8|56:6–8}}; {{Isaiah 60:1-3|60:1–3}}; {{Philippians 2:15|Philippians 2:15}}).
*Glorify your Father in heaven*: Those who pretend to be religious want people to praise them, but the disciples of Jesus should want people to praise God (see {{1 Peter 2:12|1 Peter 2:12}}).

- To *abolish* would mean to remove and replace the Law of Moses and the writings of the prophets (that is, the whole Old Testament) as God’s revelation of his will.

- *until everything is accomplished*: This could mean to obey the Old Testament perfectly, complete their teachings, or fulfill their prophecies (see {{Matthew 1:22|Matthew 1:22}}; {{Matthew 2:15|2:15}}, {{Matthew 2:17|17}}, {{Matthew 2:23|23}}). Jesus himself embodies everything the Prophets and the Law taught and expected. Now that Christ has arrived, who fulfills these writings, we must understand the Old Testament in relation to him ({{Luke 24:26|Luke 24:26}}, {{Luke 24:44|44}}).

- The fulfillment of the Law in Christ means that his disciples must obey all of his commands (see {{Matthew 28:20|Matthew 28:20}}). 

- *commandments: *This refers to Old Testament commands ({{Matthew 5:18|5:18}}) now fulfilled in Christ's teachings (see {{Matthew 5:21-48|5:21–48}}).

- *least in the kingdom of heaven: *Jesus may mean that such a person will still enter the kingdom, but only barely and with low status. Another view, based on some Jewish evidence, is that he means eternal exclusion or damnation (compare {{Matthew 8:12|8:12}}, where “those for whom the Kingdom was prepared” are shut out forever).

*Unless your righteousness exceeds: *The disciples of Jesus need a new kind of righteousness that only he teaches and makes possible. {{Matthew 5:21-47|Matthew 5:21–47}} shows this and {{Matthew 5:48|5:48}}summarizes what it is. 

This righteousness is different in amount and quality. Jesus is greater than the temple ({{Matthew 12:6|12:6}}) and Jonah ({{Matthew 12:41|12:41}}). So, the righteousness of his disciples must greatly surpass that of the Jewish religious teachers and Pharisees (see {{Matthew 3:7-9|3:7–9}}).

*it was said to the ancients*: The expression refers to the traditional interpretation of the teachers of religious law and Pharisees. Their traditions did not allow murder, but they did allow hatred. The righteous way of life required by Jesus surpasses this attitude. It demands people to live in peace with each other ({{Matthew 5:23-24|Matthew 5:23–24}}). It is not enough to only avoid committing murder ({{Matthew 5:22|5:22}}).

*You have heard … But I tell you*: Jesus contrasts his teachings to six misunderstandings of the law. Each example shows the surpassing righteousness of Jesus. Jesus reveals God's will, which contrasts with human traditions.

Jesus taught about many laws recorded in the Law of Moses. He showed what was most important about them. God is looking for people who understand what he really wants.

Jesus gave many examples of what God desires. Every example was about how people should live with others and treat one another. Jesus taught that people should love their enemies and not just their friends and neighbours.

People shouldn’t treat others based on how they themselves have been treated. Instead, Jesus taught people to look for ways to do good to others. People who do this are children of the kingdom of heaven. God is their Father and they follow his example. They take care of others and bless them.

- *Judgment … Sanhedrin … hell*: The second and third punishments are more severe than usual in the time of Jesus. This emphasizes the surpassing righteousness of Jesus and his followers (see {{Matthew 5:20|Matthew 5:20}}). They did not accept unresolved conflicts or treating other people as unimportant. 

- *anyone who says to his brother, ‘Raca’*: The Aramaic term *reqa’* (transliterated as *raca*) means something like "empty head." This probably means the same thing as cursing someone (literally *if you say, ‘You fool’; *compare {{James 2:20|James 2:20}}). Thinking that other people are unimportant is a sin that expresses itself in different ways.
Jesus provides two examples of making peace in communities and society.
The righteousness of Jesus exposes sin beyond only outward actions. He shows the true purpose of the law.

*Hell* (Greek *Gehenna*): *Gehenna* was the name of a valley outside Jerusalem. Some kings of Judah used this place to worship idols and even offered children as sacrifices by fire ({{2 Chronicles 28:3|2 Chronicles 28:3}}; {{2 Chronicles 33:6|33:6}}; {{Jeremiah 7:31|Jeremiah 7:31}}; {{Jeremiah 32:35|32:35}}). King Josiah eventually destroyed this site ({{2 Kings 23:10|2 Kings 23:10}}). 

In the New Testament, *Gehenna* refers to the place where God punishes. Jesus taught that unless his followers live with greater righteousness (living in the right way before God), they will not enter God’s kingdom ({{Matthew 5:20|Matthew 5:20}}). Instead, they will face eternal punishment ({{Matthew 5:22|5:22}}; {{Matthew 23:33|23:33}}).

*If your right eye causes you to sin, gouge it out and throw it away*: These vivid images demand a complete rejection of sin. But even extreme actions like self-harm cannot stop a lustful mind. Jesus calls for a greater righteousness that only he can provide.

*A certificate of divorce* is a document that makes a divorce legal. Evidence shows this document allowed remarriage. “The essential formula in the notice of divorce is, ‘Lo, you are free to marry any man.’ … The essential formula in a writ of emancipation is, ‘Lo, you are a freedwoman: lo, you belong to yourself’” (*Mishnah Gittin* 9:3).

Jesus challenges how people misuse the Old Testament rules about divorce (see {{Deuteronomy 24:1-4|Deuteronomy 24:1–4}}; compare {{Matthew 19:3-9|Matthew 19:3–9}}). Only following the rules does not make divorce right. Jesus permits divorce only for sexual infidelity and bans casual divorce (see also {{1 Corinthians 7:10-11|1 Corinthians 7:10–11}}).

- The exception clause allows, but does not require divorce if a spouse is unfaithful (see also {{Matthew 19:9|Matthew 19:9}}). Importantly, Jesus does not require death for the guilty person (see {{Deuteronomy 22:21-22|Deuteronomy 22:21–22}}).

- The idea is that if a man divorces his wife for the wrong reasons, he forces her into adultery by making her remarry. This would violate the law.

- *he who marries a divorced woman*: It is unclear if Jesus means any divorced woman or only those divorced without a valid reason (like unfaithfulness). Jewish divorce law assumed that legitimate divorces allowed remarriage.

Jesus explains the Old Testament's teachings on oaths ({{Leviticus 19:12|Leviticus 19:12}}; {{Numbers 30:2-4|Numbers 30:2–4}}; {{Deuteronomy 23:21-23|Deuteronomy 23:21–23}}; {{Psalm 50:14|Psalm 50:14}}; {{Zechariah 8:17|Zechariah 8:17}}). 

The Pharisees had different levels of commitment for oaths. For example, oaths not mentioning God were less serious. Jesus teaches that everything connects to God. This includes heaven, earth, Jerusalem, my head (see also {{Matthew 23:16-22|Matthew 23:16–22}}). So, breaking any oath disobeys God's command (see {{Exodus 20:7|Exodus 20:7}}). 

The main idea is to always be truthful. The teachings of Jesus make a disciple's simple "yes or no" as serious as an oath. Honest people do not need oaths ({{James 5:12|James 5:12}}).

The Old Testament allowed fair retribution (payback) ({{Exodus 21:24-25|Exodus 21:24–25}}; {{Deuteronomy 19:16-21|Deuteronomy 19:16–21}}) to keep punishments from being too severe. Yet, Jesus does not allow personal revenge for his disciples. Instead, Jesus teaches finding victory through suffering and the cross ({{1 Peter 2:23|1 Peter 2:23}}). 

Some consider this teaching as a guide for all aspects of life, including politics. Others consider it to apply to personal willingness to give up rights and forgive as God forgives (see {{Matthew 5:48|Matt 5:48}}; {{Matthew 18:23-35|18:23–35}}). Like the servant in {{Isaiah 50:4-9|Isaiah 50:4–9}} and {{Isaiah 53:7|53:7}} (see also {{Matthew 12:15-21|Matthew 12:15–21}}), the followers of Jesus should apply this virtue to honor, possessions, time, or property. True righteousness does not demand its own way.

Forced labor was a humiliating part of Roman rule (see {{Matthew 27:32|Matthew 27:32}}). Jesus transformed it into a chance to joyfully serve God. This saying shows that Jesus opposed Jewish revolutionaries, who called for violent resistance (see {{Matthew 5:9|5:9}}).

*Hate your enemy*: Jesus is not rejecting the Old Testament. Instead, he is correcting a traditional interpretation that was mistaken (see {{Exodus 23:4-5|Exodus 23:4–5}}). The Old Testament never commands people to “hate your enemy.” The closest verses are in {{Psalm 139:21-22|Psalm 139:21–22}}, where hatred is expressed toward God’s enemies.

By loving everyone, the followers of Jesus would not *become* children of God. Their actions would demonstrate that they are already God's true children, living according to his nature and will (see {{Deuteronomy 10:18-19|Deuteronomy 10:18–19}}).
*If you greet only your brothers*: Jews were taught to greet Gentiles (non-Jews) to keep peaceful relations. But such greetings were not the same as those given to “brothers,” meaning fellow Jews.

- This verse connects {{Matthew 5:20-48|5:20–48}} as a single unit (see study note on Matthew 4:23–25).

- *be perfect*: The word “perfect” means maturity, wholeness, and full devotion to God. It describes a complete response to the message of Jesus about the kingdom ({{Matthew 19:21|19:21}}; {{Ephesians 4:13|Ephesians 4:13}}; {{Philippians 3:15|Philippians 3:15}}; {{Colossians 1:28|Colossians 1:28}}; {{Colossians 4:12|4:12}}; {{1 John 4:18|1 John 4:18}}). True perfection has love at its center (see {{Luke 6:36|Luke 6:36}}).

- This verse begins the teaching in {{Matthew 6:2-18|Matthew 6:2–18}}. Jesus explains that righteousness (living in line with God’s will) should not be done for public recognition. It should be offered as service to God.

- *Righteous acts* are actions that follow God’s way of living. Examples include:

- giving gifts to those in need ({{Matthew 6:2-4|6:2–4}}), 

- praying ({{Matthew 6:5-15|6:5–15}}), and 

- fasting ({{Matthew 6:16-18|6:16–18}}). 

Jesus encourages keeping these actions private to avoid seeking personal praise instead of honoring God (compare {{Matthew 5:16|5:16}}).

Jesus talked about what being holy means and about what holy living means. He taught that God should be at the centre of people’s thoughts and actions.

God sees when his children do good deeds. The reason they do good isn’t so that they can be honoured by others. They do good because they want to share the wonderful things their Father provides.

Jesus gave an example of God being at the centre of people’s thoughts and actions. He taught his disciples how to pray. Earlier he had talked about people who were blessed in the kingdom of heaven. This prayer was an example of what those blessed people pray.

Jesus’ prayer recognised that those who follow God are part of God’s family. God’s children call him Father. They are humble and seek to honour him instead of themselves. They trust that God is the King. They long for when he will destroy evil and fully rule on earth.

They depend on him for food and all that they need. They trust him to have mercy and to forgive them. They show this mercy to others. They make peace with others and forgive others.

Earlier, Jesus was faithful to God when the devil tempted him. God will help his children stay faithful to him. He will help them say no to sin when they are tempted. God’s children trust God to save them from the devil and all who do evil.

- *The hypocrites*: see study note on Matthew 23:13. 

- *a trumpet: *they would blow these during important ceremonies, like times of public fasts.
*Your Father … will reward you*: This is true both now and at the final judgment, which is at the end of history (see {{Matthew 25:31-46|Matthew 25:31–46}}).

*When you pray*: Jews prayed regularly at 9 am and 3 pm (see {{Acts 3:1|Acts 3:1}}). They often gathered for public prayer. Hypocrites purposely chose public places at these times so everyone would notice them.
*Go into your inner room*: Jesus is not opposed to group prayer (see {{Matthew 18:19-20|Matthew 18:19–20}}; {{Luke 11:2-4|Luke 11:2–4}}). He tells his disciples not to use prayer to seek attention.
God cannot be persuaded by repeating words over and over. The Lord’s Prayer is a simple and authoritative model ({{Matthew 6:9-13|Matthew 6:9–13}}), unlike the lengthy prayers of pagans.

- *This is how you should pray*: This introduces what is often called the Lord’s Prayer. Unlike the long and repeated prayers of pagan worshipers ({{Matthew 6:7-8|6:7–8}}).

- Most Jewish prayers did not call God “Father.” But Jesus did so in nearly every prayer. The only exception is his cry on the cross ({{Mark 15:34|Mark 15:34}}). 

- *hallowed be Your name*: This means that God’s name should be honored. In the Old Testament, God’s name was dishonored when his people sinned ({{Isaiah 29:22-24|Isaiah 29:22–24}}; {{Jeremiah 34:15-16|Jeremiah 34:15–16}}; {{Ezekiel 39:7|Ezekiel 39:7}}; {{Amos 2:7|Amos 2:7}}).
The Lord’s Prayer is similar to a typical Jewish prayer called the *qaddish*. Jesus taught this prayer to his disciples as a brief summary of their new faith.

- When the disciples of Jesus pray for God’s kingdom to come soon, they are asking for his justice, righteousness, peace, and mercy to be established.

- No one rejecting the will of God can enter God's presence ({{Matthew 7:21|Matthew 7:21}}; {{Matthew 12:50|12:50}}; {{Matthew 21:28-32|21:28–32}}).

- *on earth as it is in heaven*: This probably refers to all three petitions, not just the third.

*Give us this day our daily bread*: A disciple can confidently ask God to provide for daily needs. Then the disciple can continue the work of the kingdom without worry ({{Matthew 6:25-34|Matthew 6:25–34}}).

*As we also have forgiven* (see also {{Matthew 6:14-15|Matthew 6:14–15}}; {{Matthew 18:21-35|18:21–35}}): Forgiving others shows that a person has repented and received new life from God. This makes our own forgiveness possible. Those who have experienced God’s forgiveness will also forgive. Jesus warns that people who refuse to forgive have not understood God’s mercy and may not have truly repented.

- *And lead us not into temptation*: Just as Jesus was tested ({{Matthew 4:1-11|Matthew 4:1–11}}), temptation will test a disciple's character. Jesus encourages prayer for God's help to withstand the test (see {{Matthew 26:41|26:41}}; {{Psalm 141:4|Psalm 141:4}}).

- *from the evil one*: This phrase can also be translated “from evil.” The first reading points to Satan, the one who tempts people (see {{James 1:13|James 1:13}}). The second reading points to sin in general. 

- "*for Yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, forever. Amen*": Some later manuscripts add a doxology (a short hymn of praise) at the end of the Lord’s Prayer. It was probably taken from {{1 Chronicles 29:11-13|1 Chronicles 29:11–13}} and used to shape the prayer for public worship.

People often connect prayer and fasting ({{Leviticus 23:27-32|Leviticus 23:27–32}}; {{Nehemiah 9:1-2|Nehemiah 9:1–2}}; {{Zechariah 7:3-5|Zechariah 7:3–5}}; {{Zechariah 8:19|8:19}}; {{Luke 18:12|Luke 18:12}}). Before the time of Jesus, some Israelites misused this practice ({{Isaiah 58:3-12|Isaiah 58:3–12}}).

Jesus continued teaching about God being at the centre of people’s thoughts and actions.

People care about things in the proper way only when they trust and love God.

If money and other treasures are at the centre, people serve false gods.

This turns them away from the true God who created them.

Worry shouldn’t control God’s children.

Their Father in heaven knows them and loves them.

The Creator takes care of all living things and this includes human beings.

So God’s children must trust him.

They must do what their Father wants done in his kingdom.

*Treasures in heaven*: For Jews during the time of Jesus, this was a common image. Obeying God’s commands was seen as storing up treasures with God. The context ({{Matthew 6:19|6:19}}; {{Luke 12:33|Luke 12:33}}) shows that Jesus was mainly referring to acts of charity.

- *The eye is the lamp*: The eye gives light to the body and helps guide the whole person.

- A "good" eye means a morally healthy outlook. It points to simple and wholehearted devotion to God ({{Matthew 6:24|6:24}}). Here, it also means being generous.

The word translated "money" is traditionally translated *mammon.* This is an Aramaic term for profits or material possessions. God does not tolerate rivals, so Jesus often warns about the danger of gathering wealth ({{Matthew 13:22|Matthew 13:22}}; {{Matthew 19:16-30|19:16–30}}; {{Matthew 26:14-16|26:14–16}}; {{Matthew 27:3-10|27:3–10}}; {{Matthew 28:11-15|28:11–15}}). This can become an idol (see {{Ephesians 5:5|Ephesians 5:5}}; {{Colossians 3:5|Colossians 3:5}}). We must trust God to provide our needs ({{Matthew 4:3-4|Matthew 4:3–4}}; {{Matthew 6:8|6:8}}, {{Matthew 6:11|11}}, {{Matthew 6:25-34|25–34}}; {{Matthew 7:7-11|7:7–11}}; {{Matthew 10:9-14|10:9–14}}; {{Matthew 14:15-21|14:15–21}}; {{Matthew 15:32-38|15:32–38}}). The community of disciples should support each other ({{Matthew 6:2-4|6:2–4}}; {{Matthew 10:40-42|10:40–42}}; {{Matthew 19:21|19:21}}; {{Matthew 23:23-24|23:23–24}}; {{Matthew 25:31-46|25:31–46}}; {{Matthew 26:6-13|26:6–13}}; {{Matthew 27:57-61|27:57–61}}).

Jesus taught people to live without worry by trusting God to provide for them. His disciples abandoned everything ({{Matthew 4:18-22|Matthew 4:18–22}}; {{Matthew 9:9|9:9}}; {{Matthew 10:5-14|10:5–14}}). Jesus encouraged them that God would provide their needs.

Jesus teaches by moving from lesser to greater: If God the Father cares for the birds (the lesser), he will surely care for his disciples (the greater). Because the disciples are much more valuable to him, they can trust that he will provide for their needs (see also {{Matthew 10:29-31|Matthew 10:29–31}}).
Having *little faith* comes from not understanding your worth to God and how God's favor protects you.

- *Gentiles*: This word refers to people who do not know God and do not follow his will (see also {{Matthew 20:19|Matthew 20:19}}). 

- *your heavenly Father knows*: Prayer does not give God new information about needs. Prayer shows trust in God to provide what is needed.

Here, Jesus offers a positive alternative to worrying. His disciples should focus on their commitment to God and seek his kingdom through Christ (see {{Matthew 6:19-24|Matthew 6:19–24}}). This should be their main concern.

- Mercy is a key theme in the teachings and actions of Jesus ({{Matthew 9:9-13|Matthew 9:9–13}}; {{Matthew 12:1-7|12:1–7}}). But Jesus also clearly opposes sin ({{Matthew 18:15-20|18:15–20}}; {{Matthew 23:13-33|23:13–33}}). Jesus also warns against controlling or condemning others in the name of care. The kind of judgment he forbids is often harsh criticism of small or trivial matters({{Matthew 23:23-24|23:23–24}}). Only God has the right to judge ({{James 4:11-12|James 4:11–12}}).

- *do not judge, or you will be judged*: This may refer to God's judgment at the end of time ({{Matthew 5:7|Matthew 5:7}}). God evaluates us based on how we treat others ({{Matthew 6:12|6:12}}; {{Matthew 18:21-35|18:21–35}}).

Jesus wanted his people to live holy lives full of love. He said in a few words what the entire Old Testament teaches. People must treat others the way they want to be treated. When they do, they are part of God’s kingdom coming on earth.

They are part of the community of people who believe that Jesus is the King. But some people think that God’s instructions for living give them authority to judge others. They believe they can decide who God needs to bring judgement against. This isn’t what God wants. Only God makes decisions about judgement.

His children must be humble, wise and full of mercy. That way they can help others. God has good gifts to give and longs for all people to ask for them. He wants all people to search for his kingdom and be part of his family.

Jesus encourages his disciples to serve others instead of condemning them. The contrast of a speck (speck of dust, chip of wood) to a log in the eye is an exaggerated image meant to show the huge difference (see {{Matthew 5:29|Matthew 5:29}}; {{Matthew 23:23-24|23:23–24}}; compare {{Micah 6:6-8|Micah 6:6–8}}).

- Rabbis often referred to important ideas or Scripture verses as pearls. The mysteries of the kingdom of God ({{Matthew 13:11|13:11}}) are holy (see {{Exodus 29:33|Exodus 29:33}}; {{Leviticus 2:3|Leviticus 2:3}}; {{Leviticus 22:10-16|22:10–16}}; {{Numbers 18:8-10|Numbers 18:8–10}}).

- *do not give dogs what is holy*: Jews often referred to non-Jewish (Gentile) people as dogs or pigs because these animals were ceremonially unclean ({{Matthew 15:26|Matthew 15:26}}; {{Psalm 22:16|Psalm 22:16}}, {{Psalm 22:20|20}}; {{Leviticus 11:1-47|Leviticus 11}}). Some think this means that many Gentiles would not accept the message of the kingdom. Others see it as a warning about sharing the message of the kingdom with resistant Jewish leaders (see {{Matthew 5:20|Matthew 5:20}}; {{Matthew 10:11-14|10:11–14}}; see also {{Hebrews 10:29|Hebrews 10:29}}). It could be a warning to unbelievers in general (see {{Matthew 18:17|Matthew 18:17}}; see also {{1 Corinthians 2:13-16|1 Corinthians 2:13–16}}; {{2 Peter 2:21-22|2 Peter 2:21–22}}).

This passage teaches persistence in prayer. But Jesus does not say God will fulfill extravagant desires. God's people should seek daily needs and spiritual blessings ({{Matthew 6:10-11|Matthew 6:10–11}}).

*The Law and the Prophets*: The teachings of Jesus in {{Matthew 5:21-7:6|5:21–7:6}} show the true purpose and way to express the law of Moses. Love is central for the disciples of Jesus (see also {{Galatians 5:13-14|Galatians 5:13–14}}, {{Galatians 5:18|18}}).

- *Enter through the narrow gate*: This means deciding to obey Jesus as the Messiah. The wide gate and broad road represent the choice not to follow Jesus or his teachings.

- This path leads to *destruction*. This means being thrown into fire, being kept out of the kingdom of heaven, being banished from the presence of Jesus, and finally being ruined ({{Matthew 7:19-23|Matthew 7:19–23}}, {{Matthew 7:27|27}}).

Jesus continued teaching on the mountainside. He talked about the important choice that all people face. Every person must decide between two ways of living.

They can choose the way of eternal life with God. People who want eternal life with God do what their Father wants. They are part of the kingdom of heaven. They are like healthy trees that bear good fruit.

The other way of living is to refuse God’s life. That way destroys people. Some people pretend to follow God’s ways. They say or do things that make them seem like they are God’s children. But they are like trees that bear bad fruit. Because they are doing evil, they aren’t part of the kingdom of heaven.

The Sermon on the Mount ends with a call to decide about Jesus and his teachings (see {{Matthew 4:23|Matthew 4:23}}; {{Matthew 9:35|9:35}}). Those who hear the message of Jesus about the kingdom must obey him to gain eternal life. Or else, they reject him and God will condemn them. There is no third way ({{Deuteronomy 30:15-20|Deuteronomy 30:15–20}}; {{Psalm 1:1-6|Psalm 1}}; {{Proverbs 12:28|Proverbs 12:28}}; {{Jeremiah 21:8|Jeremiah 21:8}}).
Only a few people accept the truth shown in Christ (see {{Matthew 19:23|Matthew 19:23}}; {{Matthew 20:16|20:16}}; {{Matthew 22:14|22:14}}; see also {{John 3:19|John 3:19}}; {{John 6:66-71|6:66–71}}).

*False prophets* tell people what they want to hear instead of calling them to obey God's will. {{Deuteronomy 13:1-5|Deuteronomy 13:1–5}} and {{Matthew 18:21-22|18:21–22}} provide guidelines to determine if someone is a true prophet. A prophet's words must match with God's word, and a prophet's prophecies must come true. 

Jesus explains the first rule. A prophet's actions must match his words to be trustworthy. So, a true prophet's actions will also match God's word. In the same way that fruit shows what kind of tree it comes from, a person's life shows if their inner being is good or not. 

Christians should expect false prophets at the end of time (see {{Matthew 24:11|Matthew 24:11}}, {{Matthew 24:24|24}}; {{Acts 20:28-35|Acts 20:28–35}}; {{Revelation 13:11-18|Revelation 13:11–18}}; {{Revelation 16:13|16:13}}; {{Revelation 19:20|19:20}}; {{Revelation 20:10|20:10}}). Christians can avoid these false prophets misleading them. But Christians must be careful and wise (see {{1 Corinthians 12:10|1 Corinthians 12:10}}; {{1 Corinthians 14:29|14:29}}; {{1 Thessalonians 5:21|1 Thessalonians 5:21}}; {{1 John 4:1-3|1 John 4:1–3}}; {{Revelation 2:20|Revelation 2:20}}).

Good fruit and bad fruit symbolize moral behavior (see {{Matthew 3:8|Matthew 3:8}}, {{Matthew 3:10|10}}; {{Matthew 12:33-37|12:33–37}}; {{Matthew 13:8|13:8}}; {{Matthew 21:43|21:43}}; {{Galatians 5:19-23|Galatians 5:19–23}}).
Spiritual rebirth is essential to produce the good actions that Jesus demands. Good works come from faith, and they are inseparable (see {{James 2:14-26|James 2:14–26}}).

*The will of My Father*: The teachings of Jesus show what the will of the Father is (see also {{Matthew 12:50|12:50}}; {{Matthew 21:28-32|21:28–32}}; {{Romans 2:13|Romans 2:13}}; {{James 1:22-27|James 1:22–27}}).

- *On that day*: The Old Testament concept behind this idea is the "day of the Lord." On this day, God will save the faithful and condemn those who oppress others ({{Isaiah 13:1-14:32|Isaiah 13–14}}; {{Joel 2:1-32|Joel 2:1–32}}; {{Zephaniah 1:14-16|Zephaniah 1:14–16}}). In the teachings of Jesus, this day is when everyone will be judged based on how they respond to him (see {{Matthew 10:15|Matthew 10:15}}; {{Matthew 11:20-24|11:20–24}}; {{Matthew 12:36|12:36}}; {{Matthew 24:19-50|24:19–50}}; {{Matthew 25:13|25:13}}, {{Matthew 25:31-46|31–46}}; {{Acts 17:31|Acts 17:31}}; {{Romans 2:16|Romans 2:16}}).

- Neither spiritual gifts or public accomplishments in the name of Jesus will guarantee God's approval. The decisive issue is obedience ({{Matthew 7:21|Matthew 7:21}}).

*I never knew you*: These people were never truly converted, even though they did great works in the name of God. They refused to follow the Father's will as taught by Jesus, and they continued to break Gods commands. Because they never knew Christ, they never learned to do what he commanded.

- A wise person realizes that Jesus fulfills the Old Testament promises. So a wise person willingly obeys Jesus and chooses to live in such a way that leads to blessings ({{Matthew 5:3-12|Matthew 5:3–12}}; {{Matthew 7:13-14|7:13–14}}).

- *built his house on the rock:* Building a house directly on rock provides a much stronger foundation than would a dry, sandy riverbed or floodplain ({{Matthew 7:26|7:26}}).

This entire sermon ({{Matthew 5:3-7:27|Matthew 5:3–7:27}}) focuses on following the teachings of Jesus by living righteously ({{Matthew 5:20|5:20}}). Listening without obedience is like choosing the wide gate and broad way that leads to ruin ({{James 1:22-25|James 1:22–25}}; {{James 2:14-26|2:14–26}}). A decision is necessary in light of what God has revealed (see {{Leviticus 26:1-46|Leviticus 26}}; {{Deuteronomy 28:1-68|Deuteronomy 28}}, {{Deuteronomy 30:1-20|30}}).

Jesus was finishing his long message on the mountainside. He told a story to show how important his teachings are.

People who hear Jesus’ words and obey them are like wise builders. Those who don’t listen to Jesus or obey him are like foolish builders.

Jesus wasn’t like other rabbis who only taught what they had learnt from Moses. He brought new teaching from God with great power and authority.
The storm symbolizes God's all-knowing judgment (see {{Jeremiah 23:19|Jeremiah 23:19}}; {{Ezekiel 1:4|Ezekiel 1:4}}).

- At first, Jesus began teaching only his disciples ({{Matthew 5:1|Matthew 5:1}}). But large crowds soon followed him up the mountainside.

- The teachers of religious law based their authority on Scripture they quoted or on the traditions of earlier scholars. In contrast, Jesus taught with direct authority.

He did quote Scripture in the Sermon on the Mount. Yet his words carried the weight of his own authority as the Messiah (God’s chosen one).

Jesus travelled around Galilee in northern Israel. He was known for healing people. Many who were ill came to him.

Jesus had shown great authority when he taught on the mountainside. He also showed great authority when he healed people. Jesus healed a man with a skin disease. He healed a Roman commander’s servant. He also healed Peter’s mother-in-law and people who were controlled by demons.

Matthew was showing that Jesus is more powerful than illness and demons. But God’s kingdom only comes because Jesus was willing to suffer for people. Matthew used words from a prophecy about Jesus in the book of Isaiah. Matthew showed that Jesus is God’s servant who suffers.

Here, the kingdom of God appears with supernatural power (see {{Matthew 4:23-25|Matthew 4:23–25}}; {{Matthew 11:2-6|11:2–6}}). It reaches people who were previously excluded from God's blessings. This included: 

- non-Jewish people, 

- lepers, 

- blind people, 

- sick women, 

- people possessed by demons, 

- tax collectors, 

- those with long-term bleeding, and 

- the dead. 

Jesus showed compassion to people in need. But the religious leaders reacted with anger and opposition. Jesus called his followers to respond with faith and to walk in discipleship (living as his learners and followers).

Leprosy refers to various skin diseases. People with leprosy (lepers) were ceremonially unclean and excluded from society. They could only return once they had no symptoms and a priest declared them clean (see {{Matthew 8:4|Matthew 8:4}}; {{Leviticus 14:2-32|Leviticus 14:2–32}}). Sometimes leprosy was a judgment from God ({{Numbers 12:9-15|Numbers 12:9–15}}; {{2 Kings 5:27|2 Kings 5:27}}; {{2 Kings 15:5|15:5}}).
*Be clean*: When Jesus healed lepers, it showed the presence of God's kingdom in him and his work ({{Matthew 11:2-6|Matthew 11:2–6}}).
The healed leper would show everyone that the religious leaders were wrong not to trust the Messiah ({{Matthew 10:18|Matthew 10:18}}) or that Jesus followed the law of Moses ({{Matthew 5:17|5:17}}).

- *Capernaum* is on the Sea of Galilee, four kilometers (about two and a half miles) west of where the Jordan River flows out. In the time of Jesus, it was a thriving fishing village. Located at an important crossroads on the Great Trunk Road, it connected Mesopotamia and Egypt. It was an international village. Much of the ministry Jesus did in Galilee happened there (for example, {{Matthew 4:13|Matthew 4:13}}; {{Matthew 8:14-17|8:14–17}}).

- *The centurion*: He was one of sixty commanders in a legion and led 100 Roman soldiers (see also {{Mark 15:39|Mark 15:39}}; {{Acts 10:1|Acts 10:1}}; {{Acts 27:1|27:1}}).
Jesus once again served people who were pushed aside or rejected. The centurion was a Gentile soldier. Helping him would have caused strong anger from both nationalistic Jews and separatist Jews.

*I will go* (compare {{Acts 10:9-35|Acts 10:9–35}}; {{Galatians 2:11-14|Galatians 2:11–14}}): Some scholars interpret this as a question: *Should I* [a Jew] *enter* [a Gentile's house, risking impurity]* and heal him?*

The centurion recognized the authority of Jesus. From his own experience, he knew his soldiers quickly obeyed his orders. He realized that God had given Jesus the authority to perform miracles. The centurion’s faith demonstrates that the kingdom of God includes people from all nations ({{Matthew 8:11|8:11}}).

The coming of Gentiles fulfills Old Testament promises ({{Isaiah 2:2-3|Isaiah 2:2–3}}). God promised Abraham that he would be a blessing to many nations, not just the Jewish people ({{Genesis 18:18|Genesis 18:18}}). Christ fulfills this promise ({{Galatians 3:8|Galatians 3:8}}, {{Galatians 3:16|16}}).
*with a word:* Jesus showed his powerful authority. His words alone could heal and give life.
Jesus has authority to heal every disease and rule over every demon.

*He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases*: When he took on the sins of humanity, the Messiah also carried our sickness (infirmities and diseases). Diseases exist because sin is in the world. One effect of Jesus taking our sin on the cross is physical healing ({{1 Peter 2:24|1 Peter 2:24}}). When Jesus healed people and cast out evil spirits, he showed that he is the Messiah (God's chosen one) as Scripture promised (see {{Matthew 11:2-6|Matthew 11:2–6}}; {{Matthew 12:28|12:28}}; {{1 Corinthians 11:29-30|1 Corinthians 11:29–30}}; {{James 5:13-16|James 5:13–16}}).
Jesus once met two people who said they wanted to be his followers. Jesus explained what it really means to follow him. He wanted them to understand that following him required serious commitment.

When people saw that Jesus had authority, some chose to follow him. Others made excuses not to follow him. Jesus explained that choosing to follow him is the most important decision someone can make. It can also be the hardest choice.

Then Jesus got into a boat with his disciples. The disciples were afraid when a storm came. Jesus calmed the winds and waves. The disciples were amazed that Jesus had authority over the storm. Jesus’ power brought peace to the lake.

On the other side of the lake, Jesus brought peace to two men. He drove out the demons that controlled them. The people in that town saw Jesus’ authority over the demons. They didn’t want Jesus to stay in their area.

The teachers of religious law had an honored job. They preserved, learned, and explained the Scriptures to benefit society. People thought the way to God was through them ({{Matthew 15:13-14|Matthew 15:13–14}}; {{Matthew 23:13|23:13}}).
Being a disciple of Jesus is not easy. It requires more than knowing the right things. Following Jesus includes being willing to give up life’s normal comforts.

- *Another of His disciples*: This statement suggests that the teacher in verse {{Matthew 8:19|19}} was also a disciple. Calling Jesus "Lord" shows a strong commitment to him.

- *bury my father*: In Judaism, this was a very important religious duty. But Jesus requires complete dedication to him.

*Let the dead bury their own dead*. Those who opposed Jesus might have seen these words as ignoring the commandment to honor parents ({{Exodus 20:12|Exodus 20:12}}). But it actually reinforces the first commandment ({{Exodus 20:1-3|Exodus 20:1–3}}). The authority of Jesus as the Messiah justified this statement. Living for the kingdom of heaven influences normal human life, including family ties and commitments (see {{Matthew 10:34-39|Matthew 10:34–39}}; {{Matthew 12:46-50|12:46–50}}; {{Matthew 19:29|19:29}}; {{Zechariah 13:3|Zechariah 13:3}}; {{Luke 14:26-27|Luke 14:26–27}}).

This story continues the theme of true discipleship. In the storm, the disciples had to trust Jesus with their very lives for safety and rescue. Jesus showed that he even has authority over dangerous weather and the sea (see {{Job 38:8-11|Job 38:8–11}}; {{Psalm 29:1-11|Psalms 29}}; {{Psalm 65:1-13|65:1–13}}; {{Psalm 89:9|89:9}}; {{Psalm 107:23-32|107:23–32}}).
A fierce storm came upon the lake. Sudden strong winds are common on the Sea of Galilee since mountains surround it.
*What kind of man is this?:* To receive salvation, people must recognize who Jesus is and put their trust in him. At this point, his disciples still did not understand.

*demon-possessed … so violent*: When people were possessed by demons, they often became violent. Other signs included:

- fear of the Son of God ({{Matthew 8:29|Matthew 8:29}}), 

- being unable to speak ({{Matthew 9:32|9:32}}; {{Matthew 12:22|12:22}}), 

- blindness ({{Matthew 12:22|12:22}}), 

- seizures ({{Matthew 17:15|17:15}}), 

- and doing things to hurt themselves ({{Matthew 17:15|17:15}}). 

When Jesus cast out demons, it showed that the power of God’s kingdom had entered human history ({{Matthew 12:28|12:28}}).
This event focuses on the authorityof Jesus and the cost of being his disciple. Those who have faith, like the Messiah, will experience opposition.

- Those controlled by Satan immediately recognized Jesus as the Son of God (see {{Mark 1:24|Mark 1:24}}). This answered the question asked by the disciples of Jesus when he calmed the storm ({{Matthew 8:27|Matthew 8:27}}). In other places, the true nature and identity of Jesus are acknowledged by the Father ({{Matthew 3:17|3:17}}; {{Matthew 17:5|17:5}}), Satan ({{Matthew 4:3|4:3}}, {{Matthew 4:6|6}}), people ({{Matthew 14:33|14:33}}; {{Matthew 16:16|16:16}}; {{Matthew 27:54|27:54}}), and Christ himself ({{Matthew 11:27|11:27}}; {{Matthew 24:36|24:36}}; {{Matthew 28:19|28:19}}).

- *the appointed time*: This phrase points to the final judgment. At that time, God will condemn forever all who oppose him (see {{Jude 6|Jude 1:6}}; {{Revelation 20:10|Revelation 20:10}}).
The demons could not resist the power of Jesus. They begged to escape their coming destruction.

- The words of Jesus had power to drive out demons.

- *died in the waters*: This showed that Jesus had begun to defeat the enemy ({{Matthew 12:28|Matthew 12:28}}; {{Luke 10:17-20|Luke 10:17–20}}; {{Romans 16:20|Romans 16:20}}; {{Colossians 2:15|Colossians 2:15}}).
The sad part is that people who saw the Son of God's power to save were afraid of change, so they rejected him.
Jesus lived in Capernaum ({{Mark 2:1|Mark 2:1}}). He seems to have moved there from Nazareth after the people of Nazareth rejected him ({{Matthew 4:13|Matthew 4:13}}; {{Luke 4:16-31|Luke 4:16–31}}).

A man who couldn’t walk had friends who believed that Jesus came from God. They brought their friend to Jesus.

Jesus’ work was to bring God’s kingdom to the world. In God’s kingdom, sin doesn’t control people. So Jesus forgave the man’s sins.

The teachers of the law were angry that Jesus was acting like God. Jesus has power to make people well in their spirits and in their bodies. To prove this, Jesus also healed the man’s body.

Then Jesus met the tax collector named Matthew. The Pharisees weren’t happy that Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners. Jesus explained that he had come to heal and save people who know they are sinners.

Jesus brought a new way for people to be close to God. New cloth and new wineskins were ways to describe that Jesus’ way was new.

There was debate and conflict among Jesus opponents. This included the teachers of the law and the Pharisees ({{Matthew 9:1-13|Matthew 9:1–13}}), and also the disciples of John the Baptist ({{Matthew 9:14-17|9:14–17}}).

*This man is blaspheming*: Only God can forgive sins ({{Psalm 103:3|Psalm 103:3}}; {{Isaiah 43:25|Isaiah 43:25}}; {{Jeremiah 50:20|Jeremiah 50:20}}). The teachers of religious law failed to understand the mission of Jesus as God's Son who became human ({{Matthew 3:17|Matthew 3:17}}; {{Matthew 11:25-27|11:25–27}}). As God's Messiah ({{Matthew 1:1|1:1}}; {{Matthew 11:2-6|11:2–6}}), Jesus was saving humanity ({{Matthew 8:17|8:17}}; {{Matthew 26:26-28|26:26–28}}).

It may seem easier for Jesus to say, “Your sins are forgiven,” since no one can see immediate proof. But it is much harder to heal a paralyzed man so that he can walk. The visible miracle proved that Jesus had the authority to forgive sins. It forced those who saw it to decide what they believed about him.
*So that you may know:* Jesus performed the miracle to demonstrate his authority and identity as God's Messiah (see {{Matthew 11:2-6|Matthew 11:2–6}}; {{Matthew 12:28|12:28}}).
The crowd responded with fear and admiration because they realized a powerful truth about Jesus. He is truly the Son of God with the authority to forgive sins on earth ({{Matthew 9:6|9:6}}).
Another name for the apostle Matthew was Levi ({{Mark 2:14|Mark 2:14}}). He might have had two names, or Jesus might have given him a new name.
Jesus, as Lord and Messiah, removed the obstacles that stopped righteous Jews from interacting with people considered ceremonially unclean or sinful.

The Jewish people hated Jewish tax collectors ({{Matthew 5:46-47|Matthew 5:46–47}}; {{Matthew 18:15-20|18:15–20}}). This was because they worked with Roman rulers. Jews considered them traitors against Israel. Many also considered them ceremonially unclean because of their contact with Gentiles and the images on Roman coins. 

Tax collection was a private business. In each area, Rome gave the right to collect taxes to the highest bidder (compare {{Luke 19:1-10|Luke 19:1–10}}). Collectors kept any money they gathered above their bid. Out of greed, they often used threats to get the money.

- *I desire mercy, not sacrifice*: Jesus applies this desire of God to eating with sinners. Jesus showed mercy by eating with them. This contrasted with the Pharisees who avoided sinners. They considered their avoidance to symbolize sacrifices. 

- Jesus exposed the Pharisees' true spiritual state. The Pharisees considered themselves to be righteous. But they were actually unrighteous and needed the Messiah to save them ({{Matthew 7:1-5|Matthew 7:1–5}}; {{Matthew 8:11-12|8:11–12}}; {{Matthew 19:30|19:30}}; {{Matthew 20:16|20:16}}; {{Matthew 21:43|21:43}}).
