*Fast*: Fasting was a way to show humility and repentance before God ({{2 Samuel 12:16-23|2 Samuel 12:16–23}}; {{Daniel 9:3|Daniel 9:3}}). It also reminded the nation of their need to repent ({{Leviticus 16:29-31|Leviticus 16:29–31}}; {{Nehemiah 9:1|Nehemiah 9:1}}). Some believed fasting would help bring the Messiah more quickly by purifying God’s people.

Jesus and his disciples did not fast ({{Matthew 11:18-19|Matthew 11:18–19}}) This was a quiet but clear message: the Messiah had already come (see also {{Matthew 6:16|6:16}}).

- *The guests of the bridegroom*: John the Baptist described the Messiah and his disciples this way ({{John 3:29|John 3:29}}). He used Old Testament images to show who Jesus really was (see {{Matthew 25:1-13|Matthew 25:1–13}}; {{Isaiah 54:5-6|Isaiah 54:5–6}}).

- *taken away*: This is the first prediction Jesus made about his violent death (see {{Matthew 16:21|Matthew 16:21}}; {{Matthew 17:12|17:12}}, {{Matthew 17:22-23|22–23}}; {{Matthew 20:18-19|20:18–19}}; {{Matthew 26:2|26:2}}, {{Matthew 26:26-35|26–35}}; {{Isaiah 53:8|Isaiah 53:8}}).

- *then they will fast*: Jesus might be talking about the disciples' sadness right after his crucifixion, or their way of living after his death and resurrection (see {{Acts 9:9|Acts 9:9}}; {{Acts 13:2-3|13:2–3}}; {{Acts 14:23|14:23}}; {{Acts 27:9|27:9}}, {{Acts 27:33|33}}).

These short parables compare the new covenant (the promises between God and his people) that Jesus began ({{Matthew 26:26-29|Matthew 6:26–29}}) with the old covenant. The comparison focuses especially on religious ceremonies like fasting. Jesus completes the law, but he does not cancel it ({{Matthew 5:17-20|5:17–20}}; see {{Galatians 2:21|Galatians 2:21}}; {{Galatians 5:4|5:4}}). At the same time, the new covenant brings new practices.

- *Place Your hand on her*: Placing hands on someone is a visible sign of praying for God's power to help them. It often results in new life or ministries ({{Matthew 19:13|Matthew 19:13}}; {{Numbers 27:18-23|Numbers 27:18–23}}; {{Deuteronomy 34:9|Deuteronomy 34:9}}).

- The man believed Jesus could raise the dead (see {{1 Kings 17:8-24|1 Kings 17:8–24}}; {{2 Kings 4:18-37|2 Kings 4:18–37}}).
Jesus is the Messiah with limitless power. He invites people to trust in him.

Jesus invited all people to share in the life of God’s kingdom. This included children, synagogue leaders and people who were controlled by demons.

It included blind men as well as women who were hurting. Some people saw Jesus’ powerful works and had faith. They believed that he was the Son of David. They believed he had power from God over illness, death and evil.

But not everyone believed that Jesus’ power was from God. Some of Israel’s leaders thought Jesus’ power came from the prince of demons. These leaders didn’t take care of God’s people. Jesus was different. He saw the people’s needs and worked hard to take care of them.

- Because of her constant bleeding, the woman was always considered ceremonially unclean. Anyone she touched was also unclean ({{Leviticus 15:25-30|Leviticus 15:25–30}}). But when she touched Jesus, instead of making him unclean, she was made clean. This surprising reversal shows the power to heal, redeem, and make holy (see {{Matthew 14:36|Matthew 14:36}}; {{Mark 3:10|Mark 3:10}}). 

- *fringe*: The tassels at the bottom of a tunic ({{Matthew 23:5|Matthew 23:5}}; {{Numbers 15:37-41|Numbers 15:37–41}}) reminded Jews to obey God's law.
*Your faith has healed you* (literally *has saved you)*: Her physical healing showed her spiritual salvation (see {{Matthew 8:17|Matthew 8:17}}).

*the flute players and the noisy crowd*: people publicly expressed their sorrow over a family member's death. This happened with music and laments by professional mourners. “Even the poorest in Israel should hire at least two flutes and one wailing woman” (*Mishnah Ketubbot* 4:4).

The girl had died, but Jesus said she was only asleep. He meant that she would soon be raised to life again (see {{Isaiah 26:19|Isaiah 26:19}}; {{John 11:11-14|John 11:11–14}}, {{John 11:25|25}}; {{1 Thessalonians 4:14|1 Thessalonians 4:14}}).

- Eye diseases were common in ancient times. People often considered blindness as divine punishment (see {{Exodus 4:11|Exodus 4:11}}; {{Deuteronomy 28:28|Deuteronomy 28:28}}; {{2 Kings 6:18|2 Kings 6:18}}; {{John 9:2-3|John 9:2–3}}). The Old Testament prophesies that when the Messiah came he would restore sight to the blind ({{Matthew 11:4-5|Matthew 11:4–5}}; {{Isaiah 29:18-19|Isaiah 29:18–19}}; {{Isaiah 35:5-6|35:5–6}}). 

- *Son of David* is a title connected to the Messiah and miraculous healings (see {{Matthew 1:1|Matthew 1:1}}; {{Matthew 12:23|12:23}}; {{Matthew 15:22|15:22}}; {{Matthew 20:30-31|20:30–31}}; {{2 Samuel 7:12-16|2 Samuel 7:12–16}}).
Jesus asked the question to encourage the two men to express their faith in him.
Healing the deaf so that they can hear, and the mute so that they can speak, is a sign of the kingdom of God ({{Matthew 11:4-5|Matthew 11:4–5}}; {{Isaiah 35:5-6|Isaiah 35:5–6}}).
The Messiah's actions inspire faith, surprise, and sometimes mocking rejection.

This verse links to the section that started in {{Matthew 4:23|Matthew 4:23}}. Matthew has shown Jesus as the Messiah who teaches, preaches, heals, and expels demons. Jesus calls the people to make a decision to trust in him.

Jesus expands his ministry (see {{Matthew 4:23-9:34|Matthew 4:23–9:34}}) by sending his disciples to other people in Israel ({{Matthew 10:5-6|10:5–6}}). The instructions Jesus gives his disciples ({{Matthew 10:5-42|10:5–42}}) emphasizes missionary work and the opposition and challenges they will encounter.

*Like sheep without a shepherd*: Jesus grieved the failure of the Pharisees to guide the people with care (see {{Matthew 12:11-12|Matthew 12:11–12}}; {{Matthew 18:12|18:12}}). Their constant attacks against him showed their hard-hearted rejection of God. Because of this neglect and mistreatment, the crowds suffered greatly ({{Matthew 10:5-6|10:5–6}}; {{Matthew 15:12-14|15:12–14}}; {{Matthew 23:4|23:4}}; {{Zechariah 11:16|Zechariah 11:16}}).

- *Harvest* refers to the great number of people who are ready to hear and respond to God’s message (see also {{Matthew 13:24-30|Matthew 13:24–30}}, {{Matthew 13:36-43|36–43}}; {{Mark 4:26-29|Mark 4:26–29}}; {{John 4:35-38|John 4:35–38}}; {{Revelation 14:15-20|Revelation 14:15–20}}). 

- *the Lord of the harvest*: God is the true master of the harvest. All ministries are under his call (see {{Matthew 23:8-10|Matthew 23:8–10}}, {{Matthew 23:13|13}}). So Jesus encourages his disciples to pray for God to send out more workers.

- Jesus called his twelve disciples as workers in the harvest ({{Matthew 9:37-38|Matthew 9:37–38}}). Choosing twelve was on purpose, reminding people of the twelve tribes of Israel. Jesus was appointing new leaders for God's new people under his rule as the Messiah ({{Matthew 16:18-19|16:18–19}}; {{Matthew 18:18|18:18}}; {{Matthew 19:28|19:28}}; {{Matthew 21:43|21:43}}). 

- *Jesus gave them authority* ({{Matthew 9:6-8|9:6–8}}; {{Matthew 28:18|28:18}}): Jesus empowered the twelve apostles to perform tasks that Jewish leaders could not do ({{Matthew 9:32-34|9:32–34}}; {{Matthew 10:5-8|10:5–8}}). Jesus shows his authority to cast out evil spirits ({{Matthew 8:28|8:28}}) and to heal in similar ways ({{Matthew 4:23|4:23}}; {{Matthew 8:1-9:35|8:1–9:35}}).

Jesus chose 12 of his disciples to be his most trusted followers. They were called apostles.

Jesus’ instructions to them were the second of his long messages in Matthew’s gospel. Jesus sent the 12 disciples out as partners in his work throughout Israel.

Like Jesus, the disciples were to take care of people who were suffering. They were to preach about how Jesus was bringing God’s kingdom. They were to show this was true by doing miracles like Jesus did. These included healing people’s bodies and driving out demons.

The 12 disciples weren’t to take money or extra clothes or supplies with them. God’s people should provide for the needs of God’s workers.

- The *apostles* are ambassadors sent by Christ's authority to represent him and complete specific tasks (see {{Matthew 10:1-8|Matthew 10:1–8}}, {{Matthew 10:40|40}}; {{Matthew 28:16-20|28:16–20}}). The term *apostle* also refers to Paul ({{Galatians 1:1|Galatians 1:1}}). 

- *first Simon, called Peter*: Peter was the first apostle chosen by Jesus ({{Matthew 4:18-22|Matthew 4:18–22}}; {{Matthew 16:17-19|16:17–19}}). He served as the leader of the apostles (see {{Matthew 19:27|19:27}}; {{Matthew 26:33|26:33}}; {{Acts 2:14|Acts 2:14}}).

The New Testament contains four lists of the apostles (see also {{Mark 3:16-19|Mark 3:16–19}}; {{Luke 6:14-16|Luke 6:14–16}}; {{Acts 1:13|Acts 1:13}}). These lists are slightly different.

The order of names changes, but the groups remain the same. The main difference is between “Thaddaeus” ({{Matthew 10:3|10:3}}; {{Mark 3:18|Mark 3:18}}) and “Judas son of James” ({{Luke 6:16|Luke 6:16}}; {{Acts 1:13|Acts 1:13}}). These may be two names for the same person.
Matthew, the tax collector (see {{Matthew 9:9|Matthew 9:9}}), is also known as Levi ({{Mark 2:14|Mark 2:14}}).

- *the Zealot*: Zealots were militant Jews who believed violence and war could achieve God's will. As a Jewish nationalist, Simon was probably passionate about the law ({{Acts 22:3-5|Acts 22:3–5}}; {{Galatians 1:14|Galatians 1:14}}; {{Philippians 3:6|Philippians 3:6}}). The Jewish historian Josephus blamed the Zealot party for the major war with Rome from AD 66–70. 

- *Iscariot* might refer to someone from Kerioth in southern Judea ({{Joshua 15:25|Joshua 15:25}}) or from Kerioth in Perea ({{Jeremiah 48:24|Jeremiah 48:24}}).

- *Do not go onto the road of the Gentiles*: At this time, the mission of Jesus was limited to the Jews ({{Matthew 15:24|Matthew 15:24}}). God would reach Gentiles (non-Jewish people) through the Jews ({{Isaiah 2:2-4|Isaiah 2:2–4}}; {{Isaiah 42:6-7|42:6–7}}; {{Isaiah 49:6|49:6}}; {{Isaiah 60:3|60:3}}). 

- Jews saw *Samaritans* as impure Jews ({{Luke 17:18|Luke 17:18}}) because they married gentiles during and after the Assyrian and Babylonian exiles ({{2 Kings 17:24-41|2 Kings 17:24–41}}). The tension between Jews and Samaritans grew worse in 128 BC when John Hyrcanus, a Jewish leader, destroyed the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim (Josephus, *Antiquities* 13.9.1).
They are *lost* because their shepherds (leaders) neglected them ({{Matthew 9:36|9:36}}; {{Matthew 15:24|15:24}}).
By doing these things in the name and authority of Jesus, the apostles showed that Jesus is the Messiah (see {{Matthew 11:2-6|11:2–6}}).

*Freely you have received; freely give:* While payment is not wrong ({{1 Corinthians 9:3-19|1 Corinthians 9:3–19}}; {{Galatians 6:6|Galatians 6:6}}; {{1 Timothy 5:17|1 Timothy 5:17}}), Jesus encouraged the apostles to avoid appearing greedy (see {{Acts 8:20|Acts 8:20}}; {{Acts 20:33|20:33}}).

Jesus' disciples should trust God to provide ({{Matthew 6:11|6:11}}, {{Matthew 6:25-34|25–34}}; {{Matthew 7:7-11|7:7–11}}). They should avoid greed, which could harm God's reputation. They should also encourage new communities to provide what their leaders need (see {{1 Corinthians 9:3-19|1 Corinthians 9:3–19}}).
*greet its occupants*: Greetings meant more than just saying "hello." They often included a blessing for the person receiving it (see {{Ruth 2:4|Ruth 2:4}}).

- A *worthy home *would accept the message about Jesus and the kingdom of heaven ({{Matthew 10:37-38|10:37–38}}; {{Matthew 22:8|22:8}}). 

- The disciples’ blessing was an offer of salvation. Taking back the blessing was a sign of judgment as the offer was removed.

*Shake the dust off your feet*: This act was like the actions of a prophet. It came from an Israelite custom: when crossing back into Israel, they would shake off the dust of Gentile lands to show rejection of ungodliness.

For the disciples, the gesture meant rejecting those who opposed God’s work (see {{Acts 18:6|Acts 18:6}}). Speaking judgment on those who refuse the message was part of proclaiming the good news about God’s kingdom (see {{Matthew 11:20-24|Matthew 11:20–24}}; {{Matthew 13:10-15|13:10–15}}; {{Matthew 23:37-39|23:37–39}}; {{Matthew 24:1-36|24:1–36}}).

- God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah because of their evil actions ({{Genesis 18:16-19:29|Genesis 18:16–19:29}}). With the fuller revelation through Jesus Christ, a town that rejected the disciples' message would receive a more severe judgment. 

- *that town*: A whole village or city is responsible when most people reject the message (see {{Acts 13:45-47|Acts 13:45–47}}, {{Acts 13:50-51|50–51}}; {{Acts 14:1-7|14:1–7}}). But God will save individuals who trust in him (for example, Lot; see {{Genesis 19:1-29|Genesis 19:1–29}}; {{2 Peter 2:6-9|2 Peter 2:6–9}}).

- Scripture often compares false leaders who exploit people’s spiritual weakness, instead of giving proper care, to wolves ({{Ezekiel 22:27|Ezekiel 22:27}}; {{Zephaniah 3:3|Zephaniah 3:3}}; compare {{Proverbs 28:15|Proverbs 28:15}}). 

- *be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves*: This proverb means to be wise and careful, but not deceitful or violent.

Jesus explained that following him could be very hard. His disciples needed to love him more than they loved anyone else. They must love him even more than they loved their families.

This meant that their relationship with Jesus was more important than any other relationship. Many people opposed Jesus. If the disciples remained faithful to him, they would be opposed and treated badly too.

Some of their family members would turn against them because of their faith in Jesus. People might also harm the disciples’ bodies. But the real danger was if they stopped following Jesus. Then they would lose life together with him in God’s kingdom. This would be worse than losing their families or their safety.

Jesus reminded them how deeply God cared for them and was protecting their souls. Finding life with Jesus is worth giving up everything.

Just as God gave Moses a spokesman in Aaron ({{Exodus 4:10-17|Exodus 4:10–17}}), God would also give Jesus disciples the right words at the right time through the Spirit ({{John 14:26|John 14:26}}; {{Acts 4:8|Acts 4:8}}).

- Jewish people often connected family conflict with the end times (see {{Matthew 24:9-10|Matthew 24:9–10}}). Jesus himself went through such conflict ({{Matthew 12:46-50|12:46–50}}). 

- The* one who perseveres to the end* means those who stay loyal to Jesus, even to death or until he returns ({{Matthew 10:23|10:23}}). 

- *will be saved*: Some interpret this as being freed from persecution, like release from prison. But here it refers to eternal salvation for those who stay faithful.

- *before the Son of Man comes*: Scholars disagree on whether this refers to Christ's second coming for his church or an earlier judgment, specifically the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 (see {{Matthew 16:28|16:28}}). 

- *you will not reach*: Jesus might mean “before you have *fled* through all the towns” or “before you have *spread the gospel* in all the towns.” The focus on persecution in the context (see {{Matthew 10:17-39|10:17–39}}) supports the first idea. It suggests the towns were like cities of refuge ({{Numbers 35:9-32|Numbers 35:9–32}}). This emphasizes how widely they will reject the message. It means “not until the whole nation has expelled you.”

In the time of Jesus, people often called Satan "the prince of demons." The Greek word used is *Beelzeboul*, which comes from the name of an Old Testament pagan god, Baal-zebul (“lord, the prince”). In the Latin Bible, the name appears as *Beelzebub*. This form reflects a Hebrew phrase meaning “lord of flies.” It was likely a Jewish insult against Baal-zebul (see {{2 Kings 1:2|2 Kings 1:2}}).

- The disciples of Jesus should only fear God by obeying him and testifying about him. Unlike human authorities, God's authority and judgment have no limits. 

- *hell*: See study note on Matthew 5:29.
God cares for every sparrow. So, the disciples of Jesus, who are more valuable, should not fear. God will take care of them.

God accepts those who publicly acknowledge Jesus in times of trial and persecution ({{Matthew 10:16-25|Matthew 10:16–25}}). These verses describe a person’s overall way of life, not just a single confession or denial (see {{Matthew 7:13-27|7:13–27}}). For example, Judas sometimes acknowledged Jesus but was still condemned ({{Matthew 26:23-24|26:23–24}}). Peter denied Jesus (see {{Matthew 26:69-75|26:69–75}}), but he was restored and saved.

Jesus did bring peace ({{John 14:27|John 14:27}}), but not the kind of social or political peace people often expect. Instead, he called people to make a decision about him. This decision would bring a sword, meaning division, even within families (see {{Matthew 8:21-22|Matt 8:21–22}}; {{Matthew 12:46-50|12:46–50}}; {{Luke 12:51|Luke 12:51}}).
Being loyal to Jesus is more important than being loyal to family.

The cross was a tool used by the Romans for torture and execution ({{Matthew 27:27-55|Matthew 27:27–55}}). To *take up your cross and follow* Jesus means loving him more than anything else. It also means being ready to obey him, no matter the physical or social consequences.

- *a prophet’s reward:* This can mean either the same reward a prophet gets or the benefits of a prophet's service. 

- *a righteous man*: This is someone who follows God’s law as taught by John the Baptist ({{Matthew 21:32|Matthew 21:32}}) and Jesus (see {{Matthew 3:15|3:15}}). This is why God approves of them ({{Matthew 13:43|13:43}}, {{Matthew 13:49|49}}; {{Matthew 25:37-46|25:37–46}}).

*One of these little ones: *This probably refers to the low social status of most of the disciples of Jesus (see {{Matthew 5:3|Matthew 5:3}}; {{Matthew 18:1-5|18:1–5}} and {{Matthew 6:5|6:5}}; {{Matthew 23:5-12|23:5–12}}).
